h1:
Emerald Pool & Klong Thom Hot Spring
A Full Day of Natural Soaking in Krabi
intro: Krabi isn't only beaches and islands. Inland, deep in the Klong Thom district, there's a forest hiding the Emerald Pool — water so clear and green it looks like glass — and a hot spring where mineral pools let you sit and soak warm in the middle of the jungle. It's a nature day that feels like a different world from the coast. We went ourselves and put together the full picture: the spots worth your time, the ones that might disappoint, entry fees, opening hours, and how to get there from Ao Nang or town.

blocks.html: If you've spent a few days in Krabi and the beaches are starting to blur together, a land day in the Klong Thom district is a great change of pace. The two main spots sit close together: the Emerald Pool (along with the Blue Pool spring that feeds it) and the Klong Thom Hot Spring. Both are inside the Khao Pra-Bang Khram Wildlife Sanctuary, about 50–60 km from Krabi town, roughly a 1-hour drive. Most people do both in a single day, then add Wat Tham Suea or Khao Phanom Bencha if they still have the energy.

blocks.text: Emerald Pool — Clear Green Water in the Jungle

blocks.html: The Emerald Pool (Sa Morakot / Sa Kaew) is a natural basin of emerald-green water formed where an underground spring mixes with minerals in the limestone bedrock. The result is water clear enough to see the sandy bottom, with an unusual blue-green tint. From the car park you walk about 800 m to just over 1 km on a forest trail to reach the pool. The path is shaded and easy — concrete sections alternating with wooden bridges, nothing too steep.

The water in the Emerald Pool is faintly warm and you can wade in — it's about waist to chest deep, with a marked-off swimming area. At times the water is clear enough for genuinely lovely photos, but I'll be straight with you: the clarity depends on the time of day and recent rain. After rainfall or when lots of people are wading in, the water turns murky and far less green. A lot of the disappointed reviews are simply from people who showed up on a cloudy-water day.

items: Entry fee: Thai adults 20 THB, children 10 THB · foreign adults 200 THB, children 100 THB
Opening hours: Daily 08:30–16:30 (arrive before midday so the water is still clear and the crowds are thin)
Walking distance: Car park to Emerald Pool is about 800 m–1 km; another 400–600 m on to the Blue Pool
Facilities: Changing rooms, toilets, food and souvenir stalls near the entrance

blocks.title: Go early for clearer water
blocks.html: If you want the poster-perfect clear green water, get there at the 08:30 opening. There are still few people around, the water hasn't been stirred up yet, and the morning light filtering through the leaves onto the pool is lovely. Once it gets later and more people start wading in, the water clouds up fast.

blocks.text: The Blue Pool — The Bright Spring Source That Closes in the Rainy Season

blocks.html: Walk on past the Emerald Pool another 400–600 m and you reach the Blue Pool — the source of that emerald stream. It's a small pool, roughly 15–20 m across, with water a deeper, more intense blue than the Emerald Pool, coloured by mineral sediment beneath the surface. Swimming is not allowed here — it's a conservation area and the bottom is dangerous quicksand. You can only view and photograph it from the edge.

blocks.title: The Blue Pool closes in the rainy season
blocks.html: The Blue Pool is usually closed from May to October each year to protect the breeding season of the rare Gurney's pitta. If you come in the rainy season specifically to see the Blue Pool, you may not get in — it's worth calling the sanctuary office to check first. The Emerald Pool stays open as normal.

blocks.text: Klong Thom Hot Spring — Limestone Pools to Soak In

blocks.html: About a 15–20 minute drive from the Emerald Pool is the Klong Thom Hot Spring. What makes it special is that it's a waterfall where the water is actually hot, cascading down in tiers. Over time each tier has eroded the limestone into bathtub-shaped basins about 1–1.5 m deep, with water around 40–50°C (averaging about 42°C). There's a faint trace of sulphur in the water, and it's comfortable to sit and soak in — like an onsen in the jungle. It's the only hot-water waterfall of its kind in Thailand.

The popular way to do it is to soak in the upper hot pools until you're warm, then dip into the cool stream below, alternating back and forth. Your body ends up feeling refreshed, like a spa. From the car park it's about a 400 m walk to the waterfall — the path is easy, with handrails on the sections going down to the pools.

items: Entry fee: Thai adults 20 THB · foreigners around 90–160 THB (similar to the Emerald Pool)
What to bring: Wear a swimsuit or clothes you don't mind getting wet, plus non-slip rubber shoes — there are changing rooms and toilets
Watch your footing: The limestone underwater is very slippery — walk slowly and ease yourself down; don't run or jump

blocks.title: Don't soak for too long
blocks.html: Water at 40–50°C, soaked in for tens of minutes at a stretch, can leave you light-headed or drained — especially if you have high blood pressure or a heart condition. Soak in short stretches, come up to rest, and drink water. Young children and pregnant women should avoid the hottest pools.

blocks.text: Khao Phanom Bencha — Krabi's Highest Peak

blocks.html: If you want a more serious nature fix, Khao Phanom Bencha National Park has a summit of about 1,397 m — the highest point in Krabi province. The park is on the opposite side from Klong Thom (north of town, about 20 km from the city). The easy highlight is Huay To Waterfall, a multi-tier falls about 500 m from the park headquarters, each tier with a clear pool to play in. The adventurous can do an overnight trek to the summit (a guide and park ranger are required).

items: Park entry fee: Thai adults 20 THB · foreigners 100 THB · car around 30 THB
Location: North of Krabi town, about a 20 km drive (a different route from Klong Thom)
Best for: Hikers, waterfall swimmers and nature lovers — more than people who just want quick photos

blocks.html: I'll be honest: if you're short on time, Khao Phanom Bencha isn't a must-rush on a first trip, because it's in the opposite direction from the Emerald Pool and Hot Spring, which means a lot of extra driving. It suits people with several days who especially love hiking. On a single day, focus on Klong Thom first.

blocks.text: A Klong Thom Day — The Full-Day Plan

blocks.html: This is the smoothest order for a nature day trip: leave early from Ao Nang or town, catch the Emerald Pool while the water is still clear, then soak at the hot spring in the afternoon, finishing with Wat Tham Suea on the way back.

blocks.label: All day
blocks.title: Emerald Pool → Hot Spring → Wat Tham Suea

items.note: Drive yourself or arrange a car/tour — about 50–60 km, roughly 1 hour

items.activity: Arrive at the Emerald Pool, walk in
items.note: Get there early while the water is still clear and the crowds are thin; walk on to the Blue Pool if it's open

items.activity: Wade in, take photos, rest and rehydrate
items.note: Water is about waist to chest deep with a marked-off area — keep valuables in a waterproof bag
There are southern Thai restaurants and made-to-order spots along the road before the hot spring

items.activity: Arrive at the hot spring, soak in the limestone pools
items.note: Alternate the hot pools with the cool stream, soaking in short stretches — don't overdo it

items.activity: Stop at Wat Tham Suea (if you have the energy)
items.note: Climb the 1,237 steps to the summit viewpoint, or just walk the caves at the bottom
Reach Ao Nang around dusk — just in time to shower and head out for dinner

blocks.text: How to Get to Klong Thom

blocks.html: The Emerald Pool and Hot Spring are outside town with no direct public transport. There are three main options depending on your budget and how much convenience you want.

items.name: Rent a car and drive
items.blurb: The most freedom — you control your own timing and can do the Emerald Pool, Hot Spring, plus Wat Tham Suea and Khao Phanom Bencha as you like. A sedan rental starts around 800–1,200 THB/day including insurance, and the route is on main roads that are easy to drive.

items.name: Book a day trip
items.blurb: A tour combining the Emerald Pool, Hot Spring and Wat Tham Suea, with hotel pickup, runs about 900–1,200 THB/person (some entry fees not included). Good if you'd rather not drive.

items.name: Private car + driver
items.blurb: Charter a car with a driver for a half or full day, starting around 1,500–2,500 THB/day depending on distance. Worth it for a group — split between several people it works out cheaper per head than a tour.

items: From Ao Nang: about 55–60 km, roughly 1 hour to 1 hour 15 min
From Krabi town: about 45–50 km, roughly 50 min to 1 hour
From Krabi Airport: about 45 km, roughly 1 hour (on the way back you can stop at Klong Thom before reaching town)

blocks.title: Pack the right gear
blocks.html: Bring a swimsuit, a towel, non-slip rubber shoes, a waterproof pouch for your phone, drinking water and cash (entry fees are cash only). Mosquito spray helps too, since you're in the forest. Flip-flops slip easily around the hot spring — switch to rubber shoes to be safer.

blocks.text: Worth It? Who'll Love It, Who Might Shrug

blocks.html: Straight from the real reviews: the Emerald Pool is genuinely beautiful on a clear-water day, but some people leave disappointed because they expected the vivid green of edited photos and got murky water instead. The Hot Spring, on the other hand, almost everyone loves, because a natural hot-water soak like that isn't easy to find. Overall, if you like nature, forests and waterfalls and want a break from the sea, this day is well worth it. But if you're only in Krabi for 2 days and came for the islands, you can skip it for now.

items: Great if: you have 3+ days, love nature, want to soak in a hot spring, are tired of the beaches, or are travelling with family
You can skip it if: you're in Krabi only briefly and focused on islands and diving, or you're here in the rainy season when the Blue Pool is closed
Best time to go: the dry season, Nov–Apr, when the water is clearer and the Blue Pool is open — avoid long holiday weekends when it's packed

faq.q: Are the Emerald Pool and Klong Thom Hot Spring enough for one day?
faq.a: Easily. Both are in the Klong Thom district, just a 15–20 minute drive apart. Most people do the Emerald Pool in the morning, have lunch, then soak at the Hot Spring in the afternoon. If you still have energy, you can add Wat Tham Suea on the way back.

faq.q: How much is entry to the Emerald Pool and Hot Spring?
faq.a: For the Emerald Pool, Thai adults pay 20 THB and children 10 THB; foreign adults 200 THB and children 100 THB. For the Hot Spring, Thais pay around 20 THB and foreigners around 90–160 THB. Pay in cash at each entrance.

faq.q: Is the Blue Pool open all year?
faq.a: No. The Blue Pool is usually closed from May to October each year to protect the breeding season of the rare Gurney's pitta. If you specifically want to see the Blue Pool, avoid the rainy season or call the sanctuary office to check first. The Emerald Pool stays open all year.

faq.q: How hot is the Klong Thom Hot Spring, and how long can you soak?
faq.a: The water is around 40–50°C, averaging about 42°C, comfortable to soak in like an onsen. But don't stay in for tens of minutes at a stretch — soak in short bursts, alternating with the cool stream. People with high blood pressure, heart conditions, pregnant women and young children should take extra care.

faq.q: Which month is best for clear water at Klong Thom?
faq.a: The dry season, roughly November to April, has clearer water and the Blue Pool is open. In the rainy season the water tends to be murky from sediment washing into the pool. Aim to arrive at the 08:30 opening too, because the later it gets, the more people wade in and the faster the water clouds up.
